ENFORCEABILITY OF AN ARBITRATION AGREEMENT COVERING A WRONGFUL-TERMINATION CLAIM: THE ARMENDARIZ MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS, UNCONSCIONABILITY, AND SEVERANCE (CODE CIV. PROC. §§ 1281.2, 1281.97, 1281.98; CIV. CODE § 1670.5; ARMENDARIZ V. FOUNDATION HEALTH PSYCHCARE SERVICES; LITTLE V. AUTO STIEGLER; OTO, L.L.C. V. KHO; RAMIREZ V. CHARTER COMMUNICATIONS) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes the standards California law applies when a court is asked to enforce a pre-dispute arbitration agreement against an employee’s wrongful-termination or discrimination claim: the minimum procedural requirements a mandatory employment arbitration agreement must satisfy, the general contract defense of unconscionability as it applies to such agreements, what a court may do when part of an agreement is unconscionable, and the statutory consequence of a drafting party’s failure to pay arbitration fees on time. It is prepared in connection with the separation of Jordan Lee from Acme, Inc., where the position held is stated as Field Technician, the employment is stated to have ended on July 10, 2026, the arbitration agreement is stated to have been signed on January 8, 2024, and the arbitration provider named in that agreement is stated as American Arbitration Association. Those facts are as supplied by the person preparing this sheet; nothing here verifies them or reflects any review of the actual agreement. This sheet describes published statutes and California Supreme Court decisions. It is not a petition to compel arbitration, not an opposition to one, not a demand for arbitration, not a court filing, and not a determination that any agreement is or is not enforceable, that any term is or is not unconscionable, or that any claim exists.

THE TWO STATUTES THE ANALYSIS RUNS THROUGH
Two statutes frame every dispute about enforcing an employment arbitration agreement in a California court. Code of Civil Procedure section 1281.2 tells a court what to do on a petition to compel arbitration: it directs the court to order the parties to arbitrate if it determines that an agreement to arbitrate the controversy exists, subject to the listed exceptions, which include that the right to compel arbitration has been waived by the petitioner and that grounds exist for rescission of the agreement. The same section forecloses one argument outright — an order to arbitrate may not be refused on the ground that the petitioner’s contentions lack substantive merit. Civil Code section 1670.5 supplies the defense most often raised against enforcement and, just as importantly, the menu of judicial responses to it: on a finding that a contract or any clause of it was unconscionable when made, the court may refuse to enforce the contract, enforce the remainder without the unconscionable clause, or limit the application of the clause to avoid an unconscionable result. Subdivision (b) entitles the parties to a reasonable opportunity to present evidence about the contract’s commercial setting, purpose, and effect. Whether either statute has been invoked as to Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc. is not addressed here.

THE FIVE MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS ARMENDARIZ ADOPTED
Armendariz v. Foundation Health Psychcare Services, Inc. is the decision that set the floor for mandatory employment arbitration in California. Two employees who had signed an arbitration agreement as a condition of employment sued for wrongful termination on grounds including sexual orientation discrimination under the Fair Employment and Housing Act. The California Supreme Court held that such claims are arbitrable, but only if the arbitration permits the employee actually to vindicate the unwaivable statutory right — and that for that vindication to occur the arbitration must meet certain minimum requirements, which the Court summarized as neutrality of the arbitrator, adequate discovery, a written decision permitting a limited form of judicial review, and limitations on the costs of arbitration. The Court took the list in its fuller form from the federal decision in Cole v. Burns International Security Services, quoting five requirements: neutral arbitrators, more than minimal discovery, a written award, all of the types of relief otherwise available in court, and no requirement that employees pay unreasonable costs or any arbitrators’ fees or expenses as a condition of access to the arbitration forum. The neutral-arbitrator requirement was not contested in that case; the Court treated it as essential to the integrity of the arbitration process. Whether any agreement signed by Jordan Lee on January 8, 2024 satisfies these requirements is not evaluated here.

AN ARBITRATION AGREEMENT MAY NOT CUT BACK THE REMEDIES THE STATUTE GIVES
The first of the Armendariz requirements the Court applied to the agreement before it concerned remedies. The agreement in that case limited the employee’s recovery to back pay from the date of discharge to the date of the arbitration award and stated that no other remedy, at law or in equity, including reinstatement and injunctive relief, would be available. The Court treated the underlying principle as undisputed: an arbitration agreement may not limit statutorily imposed remedies such as punitive damages and attorney fees. The employer argued the limitation reached only contract claims; the Court rejected that reading because the agreement’s final sentence made the limitation all-encompassing, and held the damages limitation contrary to public policy and unlawful. The reasoning is that an agreement to arbitrate a statutory claim implicitly incorporates the substantive and remedial provisions of the statute, so the arbitral forum must be able to deliver what the statute promises. What remedies, if any, are available on any claim arising from the separation of Jordan Lee from Acme, Inc. is not determined here.

ADEQUATE DISCOVERY AND A WRITTEN DECISION ARE READ INTO THE AGREEMENT
Two of the Armendariz requirements concern the conduct of the arbitration rather than its outcome, and the Court supplied both by interpretation rather than by refusing enforcement. On discovery, the employees argued that employers hold most of the relevant documents and employ most of the relevant witnesses, so that restricted discovery would frustrate a discrimination claim in practice. The Court agreed that adequate discovery is indispensable, and held that employees are at least entitled to discovery sufficient to adequately arbitrate the statutory claim, including access to essential documents and witnesses, as determined by the arbitrator and subject to limited judicial review under Code of Civil Procedure section 1286.2 — adding that by agreeing to arbitrate the FEHA claim the employer had already impliedly consented to such discovery, so that a discovery limitation was not a ground for holding the claim inarbitrable. On the written decision, the Court declined to state a standard of judicial review, holding only that an arbitrator in a FEHA case must issue a written arbitration decision revealing, however briefly, the essential findings and conclusions on which the award is based. Nothing in this clause describes what discovery or what form of award would be appropriate in any proceeding involving Jordan Lee.

WHO PAYS THE COSTS UNIQUE TO ARBITRATION
The cost requirement is the one that most often decides whether an employee can use the arbitral forum at all. The agreement in Armendariz was governed by the California Arbitration Act’s default rule in Code of Civil Procedure section 1284.2, under which each party pays a pro rata share of the neutral arbitrator’s fees and expenses. The employees argued that sharing arbitrator and administrative fees — which in the federal case the Court relied on ran to hundreds or thousands of dollars per day — would prevent them from vindicating FEHA rights, since a plaintiff in court pays no judge’s salary. The Court agreed and construed the FEHA as implicitly prohibiting such costs, a prohibition the default provisions of section 1284.2 do not displace. It then held that a mandatory employment arbitration agreement whose scope includes FEHA claims impliedly obliges the employer to pay all types of costs that are unique to arbitration, and added that the absence of a cost provision in the agreement is therefore not a ground for denying enforcement. What costs any particular provider, including American Arbitration Association, would charge in a proceeding involving Jordan Lee is not addressed here.

THE SAME REQUIREMENTS REACH A COMMON LAW WRONGFUL-DISCHARGE CLAIM
Armendariz arose from a statutory discrimination claim, which left open whether its requirements protect an employee suing only for wrongful termination in violation of public policy — the common law tort recognized in Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield Co. Little v. Auto Stiegler, Inc. answered that question. The employee there alleged he was demoted and then fired for investigating and reporting warranty fraud, and sought no relief under the FEHA. The Court of Appeal had held the Armendariz requirements inapplicable to nonstatutory claims. The California Supreme Court disagreed, holding that a suit claiming wrongful termination in violation of public policy is subject to the requirements set forth in Armendariz. Its reasoning was that a Tameny claim is almost by definition unwaivable because it must rest on a fundamental public policy, so an employer that cannot ask an employee to waive such a claim also cannot impose on its arbitration such burdens or procedural shortcomings as to preclude its vindication. The Court concluded that an employee arbitrating a Tameny claim has the benefit of the same minimal protections as for FEHA claims — remedies equal to those available in court including punitive damages, sufficient discovery, a written decision and judicial review adequate to ensure the arbitrator followed the law, and cost allocation that does not unduly burden the employee. The Court also addressed federal preemption, describing the requirements as applications of general state law contract principles about the unwaivability of public rights and therefore not preempted by the Federal Arbitration Act. Whether any claim of Jordan Lee is a Tameny claim is not determined here.

UNCONSCIONABILITY: TWO ELEMENTS ON A SLIDING SCALE, PROVED BY THE PARTY ASSERTING IT
The minimum requirements are one line of attack on an employment arbitration agreement; unconscionability, a defense available against contracts generally, is the other, and it applies to any arbitration imposed as a condition of employment regardless of the type of claim. OTO, L.L.C. v. Kho restated the doctrine as it stands today. A contract is unconscionable if one of the parties lacked a meaningful choice in deciding whether to agree and the contract contains terms that are unreasonably favorable to the other party. The doctrine has a procedural element, addressing the circumstances of negotiation and formation and focusing on oppression or surprise from unequal bargaining power, and a substantive element, addressing whether the agreement’s actual terms are overly harsh or one-sided. Both must be shown, but not in the same degree: as Armendariz put it, the more substantively oppressive the term, the less evidence of procedural unconscionability is required to conclude that the term is unenforceable, and the reverse. OTO also stated two limits that cut in the employer’s favor — the degree of unfairness required must be as rigorous and demanding for arbitration clauses as for any other contract clause, and the burden of proving unconscionability rests upon the party asserting it. Whether any agreement involving Jordan Lee is unconscionable in any degree is not assessed here.

ADHESION IN THE EMPLOYMENT SETTING AND THE REQUIRED “MODICUM OF BILATERALITY”
The procedural half of the analysis usually resolves quickly in the employment setting. Armendariz found the agreement before it adhesive because it was imposed on employees as a condition of employment and there was no opportunity to negotiate, and observed that the economic pressure on all but the most sought-after employees may be particularly acute, because the arbitration agreement stands between the employee and necessary employment and few employees are in a position to refuse a job because of an arbitration requirement. OTO likewise treated arbitration contracts imposed as a condition of employment as typically adhesive, and framed the remaining procedural question as whether the circumstances of formation created such oppression or surprise that closer scrutiny of the agreement’s overall fairness is required. On the substantive side, Armendariz’s best-known contribution is the requirement of a modicum of bilaterality. The Court held it unfairly one-sided for an employer with superior bargaining power to impose arbitration on the employee as plaintiff but not to accept such limitations when it seeks to prosecute a claim against the employee, and said an agreement imposed in an adhesive context lacks basic fairness and mutuality if it requires one party but not the other to arbitrate all claims arising out of the same transaction or occurrence. An employer may still justify a one-sided arrangement by business realities grounded in something other than a desire to maximize its own advantage; without such a justification, the Court said, the term is unconscionable. No conclusion is drawn here about any agreement signed by Jordan Lee on January 8, 2024.

WHAT A COURT DOES WITH AN AGREEMENT THAT HAS AN UNLAWFUL TERM
A finding that one term is unconscionable does not by itself dispose of the agreement. Civil Code section 1670.5 gives the court three options — refuse to enforce the whole contract, enforce the remainder without the offending clause, or limit the clause — and Armendariz supplied the framework for choosing among them. Drawing on the law of illegal contracts, the Court said courts are to look to the various purposes of the contract: if the central purpose of the contract is tainted with illegality the contract as a whole cannot be enforced, while if the illegality is collateral to the main purpose and can be extirpated by severance or restriction, severance and restriction are appropriate. Applying that framework, the Court identified two factors weighing against severance in the case before it. The first was that the agreement contained more than one unlawful provision — an unlawful damages provision and an unconscionably unilateral arbitration clause — which the Court said indicated a systematic effort to impose arbitration on an employee not simply as an alternative to litigation but as an inferior forum working to the employer’s advantage, so that the trial court did not abuse its discretion in concluding the agreement was permeated by an unlawful purpose. The second was that curing the lack of mutuality would have required the court to augment the agreement with terms the parties had not written. Whether any agreement involving Jordan Lee contains any unlawful term is not determined here.

On the substantive side, Armendariz’s best-known contribution is the requirement of a modicum of bilaterality. The Court held it unfairly one-sided for an employer with superior bargaining power to impose arbitration on the employee as plaintiff but not to accept such limitations when it seeks to prosecute a claim against the employee, and said an agreement imposed in an adhesive context lacks basic fairness and mutuality if it requires one party but not the other to arbitrate all claims arising out of the same transaction or occurrence. An employer may still justify a one-sided arrangement by business realities grounded in something other than a desire to maximize its own advantage; without such a justification, the Court said, the term is unconscionable. No conclusion is drawn here about any agreement signed by Jordan Lee on January 8, 2024.

expectedJSON.body: A finding that one term is unconscionable does not by itself dispose of the agreement. Civil Code section 1670.5 gives the court three options — refuse to enforce the whole contract, enforce the remainder without the offending clause, or limit the clause — and Armendariz supplied the framework for choosing among them. Drawing on the law of illegal contracts, the Court said courts are to look to the various purposes of the contract: if the central purpose of the contract is tainted with illegality the contract as a whole cannot be enforced, while if the illegality is collateral to the main purpose and can be extirpated by severance or restriction, severance and restriction are appropriate. Applying that framework, the Court identified two factors weighing against severance in the case before it. The first was that the agreement contained more than one unlawful provision — an unlawful damages provision and an unconscionably unilateral arbitration clause — which the Court said indicated a systematic effort to impose arbitration on an employee not simply as an alternative to litigation but as an inferior forum working to the employer’s advantage, so that the trial court did not abuse its discretion in concluding the agreement was permeated by an unlawful purpose. The second was that curing the lack of mutuality would have required the court to augment the agreement with terms the parties had not written. Whether any agreement involving Jordan Lee contains any unlawful term is not determined here.

expectedJSON.body: Ramirez v. Charter Communications, Inc. revisited the severance question after courts had divided over whether more than one unconscionable provision defeats severance automatically. The California Supreme Court clarified that no bright line rule requires a court to refuse enforcement if a contract has more than one unconscionable term, that a court is not required to sever or restrict a single unconscionable term either, and that the appropriate inquiry is qualitative and accounts for each factor Armendariz identified. The Court set out the order of questions: first, whether the central purpose of the contract is tainted with illegality, in which case it cannot be cured; then whether the unconscionability can be cured purely by severing or restricting terms or instead requires reformation by augmentation, since courts cannot rewrite agreements and impose terms to which neither party agreed; and then whether the interests of justice would be furthered by severance, an inquiry that focuses on whether severance would condone an illegal scheme and whether the defects show a systematic effort by the stronger party to secure a forum that works to its advantage. The Court added that although there are no bright line numerical rules, the greater the number of unconscionable provisions the less likely severance is the appropriate remedy, and that a severance clause in the contract should be taken into account as an expression of the parties’ intent though the parties cannot by such a clause divest a trial court of its discretion under Civil Code section 1670.5. Whether any of this bears on an agreement involving Jordan Lee is not addressed here.

expectedJSON.body: Separate from the case law on enforceability, the Legislature has attached a specific consequence to a drafting party’s failure to pay arbitration fees on time in an employment or consumer arbitration. Under Code of Civil Procedure section 1281.97, if the fees or costs required to initiate the arbitration are not paid within 30 days after the due date, the drafting party is in material breach of the arbitration agreement, is in default of the arbitration, and waives its right to compel arbitration under section 1281.2. Code of Civil Procedure section 1281.98 states a parallel rule for fees required to continue a pending arbitration, with the same material breach, default, and waiver consequences. Both sections require the arbitration provider to send complete invoices to all parties by the same means on the same day, and to treat invoices as due upon receipt unless the agreement states a number of days. On a default, the employee may withdraw the claim from arbitration and proceed in a court of appropriate jurisdiction, and section 1281.97 provides that the statute of limitations on claims brought or relating back to claims brought in arbitration is tolled as of the date of the first filing in any court, arbitration forum, or other dispute resolution forum. Section 1281.98 adds other elections, including continuing the arbitration, petitioning to compel payment, or paying the fees and recovering them in the award. Whether any fee has been invoiced or paid in any matter involving Jordan Lee and American Arbitration Association is not addressed here.
